story_text.value:
Using a good deal of Claude, I got OrcaSlicer (and preFlight slicer) engines running in client-side WebAssembly with a full feature set for painting, slicing, assembling, and printing 3d models.

The UI is also mobile friendly for slicing on the go.

Direct print is supported for many models, though CORS proxying is often needed.

It also supports a minimal level of TinkerCAD-style CSG modeling, as well as importing models from https://cubbycad.com

I've been using it extensively when I need to trigger prints at home from my work computer.

Take it for a test drive!

The frontend is built on Nuxt UI. GitHub repo here: https://github.com/JoshTheDerf/cubbyslicer

title.value: Show HN: A complete web build of OrcaSlicer for 3D printing

story_text.value:
I debated doing a hn post on this with myself. But the tech behind it is pretty damn cool. And I don’t have any blog posts about it or anything like that, so. I thought I’d do that here.

My son and I play a lot of modded Minecraft. We got super annoyed with hosting servers and getting mods to stay synchronized, where even a single update on the server but forgotten on the client can result in shenanigans.

So, we worked together (he’s 12) to build modrent. Users pay for their own play time (myself funding a neighborhood of players from 17-10 is gone—but I can sponsor playtime if I want to). On the hosting side, a world starts with 8 cores and 12 gb of ram running zGC. A controller then adjusts memory pressure and cpu allocations to find the optimal configuration for the server by monitoring world metrics and detecting chunk generation, etc.

Once the world allocations is less than the cost of the players currently in the world, it starts rewarding free time to the players to reduce the actual cost per player. For example, a world that costs me 0.02 per hour with two players paying 0.02 per hour, I’d reward 30 minutes to each player so they effectively paid 0.01 per hour.

Just thought I’d share it here to discuss the tech.

title.value: Show HN: Modrent Minecraft Hosting

story_text.value:
I read an article couple of years ago in a newspaper where they segmented one city based on how many schools, supermarkets hospitals etc were available in a certain area and then made a ranking based on that. The idea was mulling on my mind for a while and i finally got around making it not only for Tokyo, but for whole Japan!

Basically I gathered tons of different data sources from both freely available sources, Japan government's own open census data etc, laid them on top of the map of Japan and created weighted scores based on the results. Then based on the user's preferences (like do they want to see areas good for families, people living by themselves, do they use a car etc) it colours the map on 100m*100cm grids based on how good they are based on the values. Really good if you are for example trying to figure out a good place to live in a neighborhood and want to get a place that has a good access to supermarkets etc or even traveling a trip to the country :)

title.value: Show HN: The Livability Map of Japan
